utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before we commence, I wanted to raise one scheduling issue. I'm sure it doesn't come as a surprise to the Court that any change in the courtroom schedule has a potential knock-on effect with the witness scheduling and sometimes results in the necessity for a change in witness order, as it does in this case. Based on the information that the Court provided yesterday, and because of the lack of flexibility with respect to one witness, the previous order of witnesses following Mr. Mandic, which was to be Mr. Mandilovic, Mr. Abdel-Razek, and Mr. Mole, will be Mandilovic, Mole, and Abdel-Razek.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, everyone. Did I understand correctly that we did not admit the last document we saw yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're talking about 1D1491. I don't think it has been admitted, but to be sure ... I said the witness didn't confirm anything about the document, and so I said the Chamber will not admit this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Sorry to have brought it up. There is a decision, then. May I call up 1D1525. This is the document. The date is 5 May, 1993. Can we see the next page? It's a regular combat report to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We can deliver the translation in a couple of moments, as soon -- well, you hear the printer, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please look at the first page, and then we'll move on to the second and maybe even third in English. Can we see page 3 now? The next one. The participants we can all see, but I'm interested in the next page. It says: "Expectations of increased mortar and sniper fire, with the aim of softening the terrain, especially on the north-western part of the front." So we have certain expectations of their activity. And then it goes on to say: "The enemy is trying to provoke our units into action by firing from a distance. At about 1030 hours today, the enemy fired their own guns at the BH Presidency building in the Ukrainian Battalion Command. They tried to blame this shooting on the Army of Republika Srpska by protesting to the representatives of the UNPROFOR and the mass media." Did you know, Witness, that these things were happening?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, while I was there, I never heard of any fire against the Presidency. And by the same token, there was never any fire from the other party against Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I remember correctly whether it was you or the previous witness who mentioned the visit of Mrs. Sadako Ogata and the incoming fire from the vicinity of the Presidency, in the hope that we would return fire. But these were tricks. Even when we were not opening fire, they did, trying to blame us.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that, because we were also sometimes indirect victims of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. The witness didn't say anything about this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He did about the phenomenon in general. All right. Can we now see 1D01957 on the ELMO, perhaps, with the English translation. In e-court, it's 01 -- sorry, 1D01957. This is a letter by General Nambiar to Goulding and Vance, dated 21 January, 1993. We can see that now. Can we just take a brief look at page 2 and then move on to 3, 4, 5. This is the second page. Can we see the next one? This is a letter by General Morillon to Izetbegovic, and the subject is "Violations of Geneva Conventions by the Muslim army." Can we see the next page? This is from the 19th of January, and this one is 13 January also, "Shooting at a UN soldier in Gornji Vakuf." Again, by a Muslim. A protest letter by General Morillon to Izetbegovic. Muslim fire at the airport in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't appear on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did the witness see the previous pages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're talking about the previous pages, but I haven't seen the last one where it is mentioned regarding the runway at the airport.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope we'll see the last page now. This was the first one. Can we see the next one? That's the last one. That's the one I'm reading now again, the 19th of January. And again General Morillon, with the warmest greetings, lodges a protest with the president, and in the second sentence, it says: "At 1645 hours on 16 January 1993 ..." [In English] "At 1645 hours on 16th of January, 1993, 10 mortar rounds impacted the Sarajevo airport. Five mortar bombs landed around the northern check-point, four around the airport control radar, and the last one landed on the weather station ..." [Interpretation] And so on. In the last paragraph: [In English] "We will, of course, understand the damage that the revelation of this incident could do to your cause." [Interpretation] Did you know about these incidents and the protests lodged with Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: (redacted) But I don't recall this incident, but I'm not surprised, not very much surprised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps page 9, lines -- or page 5, lines 9 and 10, warrant redaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's clear from this that the shells were fired from Hrasnica, which is the Muslim side. Can this document be admitted? Three letters. The witness is aware of certain incidents, and the other doesn't surprise him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder about your last comment or the question. Mr. Witness, do you agree that shells were fired from Hrasnica, which was the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree that it could have happened. I don't recall this specific incident, because there were several incidents of this type. But as for this very incident, I am not surprised. And I pick up on what Mr. Karadzic was saying, saying that I was surprised. I'm not surprised by this sort of incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D351, Your Honours, perhaps under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether this should be put under seal. We redacted the certain passage in the transcript, and I don't think it should be under seal. It should be a public document. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now see 1D01960, but without broadcasting the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't see why it couldn't be broadcast, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then maybe the condition the accused has -- I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I am in favour of having everything in public, but I'm just not sure whether there could be some names here. For instance, in paragraph 3, the name of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see the point. So let's not broadcast this document, and let us move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you for your understanding. I draw your attention to the entire document. It says: "The Muslims fired on the humanitarian convoy of the Serbian Orthodox Church at Butmir airport near Sarajevo on March 5, Father Filaret of the Serbian Orthodox Church, who was in the convoy ..." [In English] "Father Filaret said that fire from all kinds of weapons had come exclusively from the left-hand side of the airport entrance, where Muslim forces have their positions." [Interpretation] And now look at the next one: [In English] "Sarajevo Television, which is controlled by the Muslim authorities, shifted the blame for the incident on the Serbs, but commander of the United Nations Protection Forces in Sarajevo," some colonel, "denied the accusation, recalled Father Filaret." [Interpretation] We skip one:

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: tonnes of flour, of which 50 tonnes were intended for Muslims and 25 each for the Serb and Croats, he said."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that convoy and the fire at the convoy?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will see that my memory doesn't always fail me, and I fully recall this incident. In fact, once everything was settled, I wanted to see for myself what the situation was, and so I went on location. And I can, therefore, confirms what it -- it's a document from the Tanjug Agency, and I believe that it confirms what I said yesterday; namely, that we really wanted to be impartial.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There's no problem in admitting this, but my question is whether we need to put it under seal or not, because I read the transcript again and the reason why this document should not be broadcast was not clear, so there's no problem in admitting it publicly. That will be done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D352.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I welcome every opportunity to have everything in public, but I'm trying to be cooperative with the measures that have been granted. Can we now see 1D465.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, while we're waiting: Is the name Jovan Divjak familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're probably talking about Colonel Divjak, who was part of the Bosnian Army and who was of Serb origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, he is a Serb still. He's not just of Serb origin. But he stayed there despite the fact that the Bosnian Army started proceedings against him.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't realise that proceedings had been started against him, but I assume that the Yugoslav Army did not see very positively that he had joined the Bosnian Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Before the war, the JNA started these proceedings, and I think that's one of the things that made him join the Bosnian Army. Can we see the next page of this document? This, as you can see, is dated 20 June, Security Administration, which is the military secret police. This is a Muslim document. It says: "The chief of security of the Guard Brigade Delta, under the influence of others in the command, wrote a letter to the commander of the Sector of the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the chief of SVK, Command of the 1st Corps, and the chief of the Security Administration, in which he, in an unclear context, makes the assumption that their brigade in the barrack Velesici is being shelled, and this is an integral part of the total effort to destroy the Guard Brigade." And at that end, it says: "The disconnect of this unit from the command-and-control system can also be seen by the fact that the security organ of that brigade, under the influence of the commanding officers in the brigade, is allowing himself to communicate with the commander of the SVK, the chief of the VK headquarters, and the 1st Corps Command." Is it clear that they carried out bombardments of their own people very often, and there were clashes not between just Caco and the 1st Brigade, but the Guards Brigade was attacked in this instance by the 1st Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is a question. Did you know that they clashed among themselves?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of those internal events. I was only aware of - how should I say it? - how the ranks of the Bosnian Army had been cleaned up from, I believe, the spring of 1993. But as for the details, I was not aware of them because I did not belong to the Bosnian Army and I did not belong to the Serb Army either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I could agree had the army been cleansed of Juka Prazina since April. Did you hear of the name Juka Prazina, General Juka Prazina? Have you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Juka" rings a bell, but I don't remember. Perhaps it's the one who was killed afterwards or perhaps in Belgium, unless I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, you're not wrong. That's precisely the man. And in April, I assume that he fled to Igman and then afterwards with the HVO -- or, rather, the HOS, but he was killed in October 1993, right, or November 1993? Caco, Caco, was killed. Musan Topalovic, nicknamed Caco, was killed in 1993, or November?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was no longer in charge at the time, but I did hear about that in my new position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, did you know that in Velesici there was a barracks for this Guards Brigade and that they had firing positions there, a tank and so on?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would have to give me more details about those barracks. The name doesn't really ring a bell, but if you give me any idea as to the unit, perhaps it will help me as to what it meant for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the Guards Brigade called Delta was over there, and this document speaks about that, that there was shooting at the barracks by the 1st Motorised Brigade with the intention of gaining supremacy in their internal balance of forces.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I'm none the wiser as to where those barracks were. It's always the same thing. I do not recall all those names, and you would have to give me more details so that I can talk more about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then I don't suppose I need tender this document; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very correct. Can we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we can do that, but I just said one name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we now have 1D456 next, please. And it's a document from Jovan Divjak, the man we mentioned earlier on, and at the time already he was most probably a general, the deputy of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That means that he was the number-two man in the army hierarchy; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I always knew him as a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. The date here -- well, he might still have been a colonel. But this is the 27th of May, 1993, and it's his resignation from the position of deputy of chief of staff, and so on, sending it to the Supreme Command and Izetbegovic, a letter of resignation from the position of deputy, et cetera, reasons for resigning. Point 1: "I tendered my resignation in May because of several violent crimes against the citizens of Sarajevo. In these incidents, Musan Topalovic's, aka Caco's, gangsters seriously wounded my son, Zelimir, in Marsal Tito Street." And then number 2, paragraph 2, it goes on to say how he wasn't treated as a deputy, but as a third man. And can we move on to the next page, please? Or, rather, we can stay with that page in the English. No, next page for the English as well and the B/C/S. The whole document is about a resignation. It's a resignation by the number-two man in the army. Now look at para 5: "I do not agree with the actions of the Staff of the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces concerning the current and the most difficult period in the liberation war so far, where nobody is taking appropriate measures to stop the criminal conduct of some military personnel. (I do not agree that these are deserving BH Army commanders) against the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina." And then he says: "I don't know who gave permission for private prisons to be set up in Hrasnica and Dobrinja." And then -- well, let me ask you: Did you know that private prisons existed? We informed the public about that, but did you know that there was a private prison in Sarajevo for Serbs?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have that type of information. I saw -- I accompanied some official persons from the outside who led exchanges of prisoners, and I had the possibility to visit two prisons, but those were official prisons which existed in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you know about this conduct or, rather, this move by Colonel Divjak, as he probably was then, this step that he took?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was aware that he did not agree with everything that was being done inside the Bosnian Army and that he probably suggested that this army should be re-organised. And he, as a professional soldier, because as I reminded you earlier on, he was a member of the Yugoslav Army earlier on, and so he wanted everything to be done according to the Rules of War.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now look what it says down there towards the bottom of the page: "Despite information about the criminal actions of the 10th Mountain Brigade available to the Supreme Command of the Armed Forces, nothing is being done." May we now turn to the next page, please. "I hereby request" is what I would like us to look at the bottom of the page: "I hereby request to be reassigned from the Supreme Command Staff to the position of soldier in the 10th Mountain Brigade of the RBH Army." And then he goes on to say: "And if you receive a report that I was killed because I tried to escape to the other side in 10 or 15 days' time, please do not believe it. I support your Bosnia-Herzegovina with all my heart and soul." So a Serb, completely loyal to Alija Izetbegovic, has some criticisms to make and says he doesn't like what is going on, and mentions private prisons, and nobody seems to want to regulate that issue. Is that what you said when you said he didn't agree with certain things that were happening in the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, and that is --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to tender this document now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yet again, I think we are having some technical difficult tools.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The booths can hear the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Ms. Edgerton, now? [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [B/C/S spoken]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objection, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I actually didn't hear you at that moment, Your Honour. That's why I asked you to say something, and I didn't hear you at that moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The booths can hear the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Like my colleague here, I can here a lot of feedback from what's going on inside the booth, actually, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's now working. Sorry for the inconvenience, Mr. Witness, again. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really question the relevance of this document in any regard; in fact, this whole line of questioning. I just -- I'd like to hear the relevance of it, if I may, Your Honour. I find it completely irrelevant to the situation, the witness's evidence, and these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to say something? I'll explain why the Defence -- or how the Defence views this. Before us, we have the 1st Corps of the BH Army, all power and authority vested there, and in that small part of town controlled by them you have terror against the Serbs and the Muslims. The city is full of soldiers, full of weapons, and full of criminals, and that has a significant effect on our conduct, the conduct of our side, because we are in conflict with the other side, and our conduct depends on their conduct. You have prisons for Serbs, you have cross-firing. This man's son -- this colonel's son was wounded. So there's general chaos, and we have to put that to the Trial Chamber so that the Trial Chamber can bear in mind what the situation was like over there. And many of those incidents are ascribed to us and we are being held accountable, and they want to show that it was -- that Sarajevo was idyllic. That's the kind of picture that was painted and has been painted so far, of an idyllic Sarajevo with only Serbs attacking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton, the Chamber is of the view that the accused can put his case to the witness, irrespective of the evidence-in-chief he'd given during the course of examination-in-chief. As such, although the witness did not cover every bit about the content of this document, he'll confirm to a certain extent the way Mr. Divjak did not agree with the way conducted by the government at the time. So we find it relevant, and we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D353, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we now have 1D419 next, please, on e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting, Witness, let me ask you this: Did you know the scope -- well, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know how much ammunition and how many weapons were actually produced in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't see you. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we have private session for what I'm about to say, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, were you aware of the scope to which ammunition and weapons were being manufactured in the Muslim part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that at all. I had no information about that whatsoever, and everything we -- I knew and that we already referred to, earlier on, was that the Bosnian Army had ammunition supplied from the outside and possibly also weapons. And, personally, while walking at the end of the day in Sarajevo, I could see that these fighters were changing guard and changing shifts, and they were not armed; that is, that the arriving people took the weapon of those who were on the front-line, which showed to me that they probably had a big problem of ammunition and weaponry. And if they had easily manufactured that on the spot, they would not have been confronted with that type of problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I tell you that in their sources, and General Divjak writes about this, that 120-millimetre mines -- that 80.000 pieces were produced in the center of Sarajevo, would you be surprised to hear that piece of information?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are saying that. Well, yes, it would surprise me, but I hope that you base that statement on a document, with value that can be granted to such document. And I would be rather surprised if this were the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you exclude the possibility? And in the meantime, may we have page 4 displayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we do not need the speculation on the part of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's look at page 4, the underlined part. It says: "In connection with the recent explosion in the -- in connection with the resent explosion at the auxiliary workshop for the loading of gun shells at the Technical School in Sarajevo, which destroyed five rooms, it is suspected that it was deliberately caused, based on information received to date, by laying explosives inside the building, or, in other words, that it was an act of sabotage. "Operative measures are being taken to solve this case."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know where the Technical School was?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only knew one technical school. At least that was the way we called it. It was the old school of [indiscernible]. But at the time I was there, this was occupied by the Serb Army. But there might have been another school called Technical School in Sarajevo, but I do not know where it was or whether it existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's the Technical School, a nice building, a nice old Austrian building, located between the Holiday Inn and the Marsal Tito Barracks. Do you remember it better now?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The place you're referring to, yes, that I can -- I remember it, but I was not aware that there was a school. I never went there, and I've never heard about it before you referred to it today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But this is their document, a Muslim document. It says that there was this explosion, destroying five rooms. And I don't doubt that they blamed us for that. So do you know that an explosion of that kind would, as a general rule, have been ascribed to the Serbs and that Serbs would be blamed for it?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Anyhow, I was not aware of this document. I remind you that I'm not a member of the Bosnian Army, so I was not an addressee of such a document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then I don't suppose you're going to admit this document into evidence. May we then have 1D1547 next, please. This is a regular combat report from the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, sent to the Main Staff on the 10th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The translation will be on the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I thank you too. [In English] Please, the first page to be identified, and then we'll go -- and then we may go to third.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a customary regular combat report, and it says what the enemy is doing. And we can now move on to the next page. They are complaining that there's no food, ammunition, or fuel. Let's move on to the next page. [In English] It must be another one next. Point 5, point 5. [Interpretation] Here we see that the command -- the corps command is once again saying that there's no ammunition, fuel, and food; that the food they do get is always the same; that many people have nothing to eat, the soldiers' families have nothing to eat. Now -- [In English] Can we get point 8, please. [Interpretation] That's right. [In English] There may be some lifting -- [Interpretation] Let's look at point A: "The Turks," it says, "are daily intensifying their attacks on all brigades with artillery, mortar, and sniper and rifle brigades. The number of projectiles fired increases every day." So the Sarajevo Romanija Corps has less and less ammunition, whereas the 1st Corps of Bosnia-Herzegovina has more and more. [In English] Can we put down there -- before point C in this forecast, that must be next: "We believe ..." [Interpretation] "We believe that the Turks in Sarajevo are being supplied with ammunition by UNPROFOR because there is no other logical explanation of their expenditure of so much of it." Now, do you know that there were suspicions along these lines?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were used to having the two parties present, that they were rather paranoid in attitude, and this is a good example of such paranoid attitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in oxygen bottles, explosives were introduced into Sarajevo, and this was confirmed by General Delic in his memoirs, and our soldiers would even load them on to another place, and he laughs in his memoirs, saying that the Chetniks didn't know what they were reloading? So explosives entered Sarajevo in oxygen bottles, with the help of the United Nations. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an incident with the transport of black powder in oxygen tanks, and that was the beginning of 1993. But as far as I know, this type of incident did not occur afterwards. The UN forces were very much aware of it and were on their guards. I just want to remind you that these oxygen bottles were transported by humanitarian organisations, especially UNHCR, and not by UNPROFOR. UNPROFOR was just escorting these convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you can only know about things you intercepted. If you didn't intercept something, then it passed?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know whether anything else passed through.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Will this document be admitted? It talks about all the various things that were occurring and relates to the balance of power in ammunition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You'll have another opportunity, Mr. Karadzic, to tender this document through another witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I ask for private session for a while, and 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- 09579.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree if I say that the media, primarily the Western media, favoured the Muslim side? They were biased?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have to cast any judgement on the media.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I call up 1D1931.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when we get the document, I'd like to ask you: Are you aware that the Conference on Bosnia-Herzegovina began in the end of 1991 and early 1992, before the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that that conference lasted continuously all the way up to the Dayton Accords, one conference after another?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was reading the press, as you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it's very important to establish whether there was a possibility of fait accompli, in view of the fact that by joining the conference, we gave up on the fait accompli option and validating military gains in that way. The war could not have given us anything outside of the conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I had a mission that I was fulfilling there. As for the rest, this was not a matter to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Edgerton, you were concerned about the previous set of question and answer?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take care of it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see further down the page just to see how things were developing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The secretary of the president of Republika Srpska, he's answering someone and says: "Dear sir. As soon as we received your letter, we placed your sister, Ljiljana, and her husband, Proko Gojkovic, on the list of people who have priority in leaving the city. Right now, nobody's leaving Sarajevo because the Muslim authorities have strengthened controls, especially after the clashes between Muslims and Croats. Whether and when it will be possible to leave the city again, we don't know, because many things do not depend on us. We will, on our part, do everything to have that happen as soon as possible." Are you aware, Witness, that the Muslim authorities did not do anything to organise departures of civilians in any civilised form?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were not refusing the departure of civilians towards the outside of the city. They were controlling, so, namely, they were letting go only those that they were prepared to let go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But if I tell you that they were not prepared to let them go, they allowed only small numbers to leave, whereas the majority had to pay criminals to take them in secret out of that territory, would you deny that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think so, but I cannot contest this either, because I have seen mafia-like behaviours within the city and outside the city, so I'm not surprised that some people were actually using the situation of high distress and they were doing some gainful exercise out of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Will this document be admitted or marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think the witness commented on this specific event, although he testified in general terms about the situation, so I don't think we have the basis to admit this one at this moment, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May I now ask for a map to be displayed. It's in e-court, actually. Can we get 1D1088.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, you are very reserved when answering my questions. You are afraid to make any political evaluations and analysis. That's not exactly the same attitude as you have to the OTP. When --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's a comment, an unnecessary comment. You put your question. Just let's come to your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to repeat what the witness said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said, Witness, that there had been a siege, and the point of the siege was to cut off power, water, gas supply, et cetera, and now I'm putting to you the next assertion. Sarajevo was a divided city. What you see before you is the broader region of Sarajevo. Both the city proper and the broader area of Sarajevo were divided. There are lines showing these separations. Now, by defending its areas, and the blue areas are Serb, were we laying siege?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there were front-lines which were established as the combat progressed, and along those front-lines there were people that were outside and then they were blocking those that were within. And the main part of it was within the city, apart from the Grbavica area of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you. You see Grbavica here, but do you see Lukavica? Do you see, in the far west, Ilidza, and a thin white line marking the city proper, which includes Lukavica and Ilidza? Those are Serb neighbourhoods in the city.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hear the accused a lot better in his original language than the translation into French, so it seems that once again we have a problem with the sound coming from the various booths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From my previous question, it was not recorded. Was that an encirclement, as you referred to it several times, or was it a siege?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the accused has a very strong voice, and it seems that he's covering the translation. So either we reduce the sound from the accused or we strengthen the sound coming from the French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One way of doing it is we take a break now, and then that matter, hopefully, can be looked at. We'll have a break for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was advised that the technical difficulties have been solved. Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. With your leave and with all due respect, I have to express my regret once again that we don't have more time, but I will try to present as many things as I can in the remaining time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, here on the right are the lists of every populated area. Every area is bordered in red. And according to the census, it was exactly established, which communities in the majority in which area, and these are almost absolute majorities. Do you see that the separation line, the front-line in Sarajevo, is more or less consistent with the ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand your question or your comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, look, for instance, at the north-west. Ilijas is there, and the Serbian part of Ilijas is in Serbian hands. Or perhaps it's better to move to the next map, 1D1081. We'll get every municipality separately, and we'll see what was controlled by Muslims and what was controlled by Serbs. 1D -- yes, that's it. Do you agree that this is the municipality of Pale?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I am not a specialist in reading Cyrillic characters, and therefore I cannot see where "Pale" is written.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's written in the middle. But do you believe me, that this is the Pale municipality?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will gladly believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that these three large green concentrations that designate the Muslim majority are not under the control of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the front-line on this map is the large black line which we see in the south/south-eastern part of this map.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we get 1D1082.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we see the Ilijas municipality, whereas the town of Ilijas, the center of the municipality, is to the far west on this picture. Do you see that, as far as possible, the confrontation line coincides with the ethnic separations?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that if you look at what is on the side of the map, it says that it's dated 31st of March, or it's based on the census from the 31st of March, 1981, which means that we are going back 12 years before the matter at hand. I know that there was quite a lot of population movements following the first conflict, so I'm not quite sure whether one could base any comments on such a document in order to make any remark or comment regarding the ethnic make-up for the date that is at hand here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since Ms. Edgerton didn't rise, Mr. Karadzic, I have to ask you. Who drew these lines in, who wrote these letters?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did that, based on the front-line. It's the separation line that we can see on all the other maps, and here they separated the zone of Sarajevo, broken down by municipalities, to see what was controlled by Serbs, what was controlled by Muslims. And this line roughly coincides with the separation line in the zone of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're right, as far as movements of population are concerned, but these are genuinely Serb or Muslim neighbourhoods according to the 1991 census, because the 1991 census was challenged, it was never verified by the Assembly, it is considered that it was falsified, et cetera. Can we get 1D1083. For your information, Your Honours, this is the same map as the previous one, but now it's broken down by municipalities, and we are adding municipalities one by one. Do you agree that what is added here is the Hadzici municipality?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that it is the correct location, if -- when trying to see more clearly the various maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree -- do you agree that the Serbs controlled just a small part of Hadzici, namely, the Serb part of Hadzici, whereas the overwhelming majority of Hadzici were Muslim, including Tarcin and another area, and Serbs did not control that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there again, the confrontation line is the black line in bold north-west or south-east, which is on the eastern side of the yellow parts. That's what you're talking about. So this is the part that's held by the Serbian forces, and this would be the blue parts with a few yellow spots. I'm trying to understand or make sense of this map as I speak. It's on the left-hand side of the map, what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I forgot to mention the blue areas are Serb, ochre is Croats, and the green are Muslims. Can we get now 1D1084.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that we now see the Trnovo municipality added? It's to the far south of the Sarajevo district.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the various pieces of the puzzles fit in together, and I believe that we will have soon come to the end of the puzzle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you see the front-line, which covers mainly Serbian parts, and some Serb areas are controlled by Muslims, and some Muslim parts are controlled by Serbs, but that the bulk of the Serb neighbourhoods is under Serbian control?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Provided that this document is accurate, because you said that some people had said, when it was published, that it had been falsified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I have to correct you, sorry. It's the 1991 census that was challenged, it was disputable, and it was never verified by the Parliament. However, this census was not in question. This was done by the previous Yugoslav authorities. Can we get now 1D1085. Do you agree that we now see Ilidza municipality, and in that municipality Serbs controlled Serb neighbourhoods, whereas the Muslims controlled Hrasnica, Sokolovic, and Butmir?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if we take on board your correction that you made and the mistake that you had made between 1981 and 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But can we get 1D1086.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we get Nova Sarajevo municipality, which was the majority, and together with the Yugoslavs they had absolute majority. Do you see the Serbs control the Serb part of the territory, and what they don't control are Pofalici, which fell in May 1992 already? Do you see that there are no Muslim areas under Serb control?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that there's some blue. I can see that there's no yellow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we now have 1D1087, please. We'll probably be seeing Stari Grad now. That's right, Stari Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And there the population is mostly Muslim, and most of Stari Grad, the Old Town, is under Muslim control or, rather, within the separation line on the Muslim side; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we now have 1D1088 next, please. This is the center? No, it isn't, no, or maybe. Just a moment. Let me check.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now we see that same situation, the same picture, where all the pieces of the puzzle have been put together. Now, Witness, do you accept that the Serb population living here in this area, in the blue zones, has always lived there, and that it is the oldest population in that area of Sarajevo? And let me tell you why I'm asking you that; because it was portrayed as if we had come in from somewhere and set up the siege of Sarajevo. That's the impression that has been gained through the media and through the various trials here. But this is the autochthonous population which has lived there since time immemorial. It's their land, and it was never otherwise. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The question calls for speculation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's see whether Mr. Witness can answer the question or whether he's aware of the situation without relying on his speculation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have two comments to make, Your Honour. The first one is the following: The accused uses a document with an authenticity that has not been ascertained. And the second comment is that I'm no historian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can you confirm it? Well, you've already confirmed it, that the soldiers who were in the Army of Republika Srpska lived there, the ordinary people who went about their business and then went up to the front-line when needed; right?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about the ethnic make-up of Sarajevo. From what I could see, Sarajevo was typical for having a mix of populations, and within the city, even during the siege, there was a very strong Serbian minority. And at the time, we thought that it was about 16.000 or 17.000 [as interpreted] Serbs out of 250.000 or 300.000 inhabitants. As for the Serb soldiers that I saw outside of the confrontation lines, so those that were taking part in the siege of Sarajevo, some were coming from Sarajevo, but they would certainly not go back there every day or every evening to sleep there or to carry out their business as civilians. I have to say that I spoke to some Serb soldiers who were reservists, and they were born in Sarajevo, and they were very sorry that they could not go back home. I have not seen lots of them, but those that I met told me that. So this is what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For your information, when you were there, there were about 50.000 Serbs, and by the end of the war, 30.000 Serbs remained. Now there are just a dozen -- 12.000 of them or 10.000. But let's see this, Witness: If these people living here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, again.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's just about these comments for the witness's information, which are unhelpful, waste time, and, in my submission, inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I can't agree more. Mr. Karadzic, be cautious.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But do you accept that when you were there, there might have been 50.000 Serbs in that part of Sarajevo controlled by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier on, I had a more optimistic view of things. I spoke of 60.000, 70.000 or so, but there might have been 50.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then I apologise, because the interpretation I received was that you said 16, not 60. But that makes it roughly about the same figure. About 50.000, 60.000. Yes, I agree. Now, tell me this Witness: When the Serbs, in April 1992, set up these lines to protect their settlements, was it the Muslims under siege, or was it the Serbs who were under siege by the Muslims, or was the third variant correct whereby it was a divided city?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If, as you said earlier on, we are speaking about the city, itself, Sarajevo proper, as the Brits would say, the city itself, the center of Sarajevo, the main center of Sarajevo, plus the modern part close to the airport, they were besieged and they were surrounded. And so when you say that they were surrounding and there was no siege, it is a subtle nuance which I must say I do not quite see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you see that the person compiling this map considers Ilidza to be the narrower part of town, and a witness in another trial here - she was a distinguished British journalist - said that it was a town -- a city divided, not a city under siege? And would you agree with that, that it was a city divided, because we can see that the separation lines and the confrontation lines enter all the pores of the city, both the inner city and the surrounding parts?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If, to your mind, you say that Pale was part of Sarajevo, then, of course, there is a division. But I think that that is an extension of the notion of Sarajevo, which is going too far.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope you'll believe me that this is the district of Sarajevo, and the inner-city is divided, just like the outer city. But, anyway, thank you, and I would like to tender this document, all these eight slides, the whole set from 1081 to 1088.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Chairman, as Mr. Karadzic said earlier on, I think that we will need to correct what was written down in the minutes, because there was an error made in the figures I quoted. It was 60, 6-0, 60.000, and 70.000 and not 16 and 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your comment. The court reporters will look into the matter. Thank you very much. I thought you were dealing with it as kind of submissions, but I will benefit from hearing from Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I had noted it as well, Your Honour, but I -- unless it's something that I think is really necessary to bring to Your Honour's attention, I generally deal with it when we look at the draft transcript later on. In any case, listening to the witness, I noted "60 to 70.000" in French, as opposed to "16 to 17," which appeared on the English language transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, I was asking you about your opinion as to the admissibility of these maps, annotated by the accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, the witness had no comment on them and was at pains to distance himself from them, saying he doubted the authenticity and, further, he's wasn't a historian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In particular, Mr. Karadzic, given that it was marked by yourself, so we are minded to admit them when you are giving testimony. Otherwise, at this moment I don't think it's appropriate for us to admit them as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But there will be witnesses who will authenticate them, I hope. Right? Now may we have 1913 next, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness, we're going to see a map showing part of the distribution of Muslim forces in the city, itself. And a previous witness confirmed that that was just one part, that there's more but this is just one part.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, just with --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. It's a mistake. I apologise. 1D1293 is the correct number.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And with respect to page 38, lines 5, 6 and 7, I don't know that that's evidence before the Court at all, Your Honour. I'd like to see where that might have taken place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have 1D1293, and we showed that to one of the first witnesses who testified, and they said -- well, we'll deal with that later, but let's have another document up on the ELMO now. Or, rather, this is on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that is another comment. What other witnesses testify, in what direction, has no bearing upon the evidence of the current witness, so please refrain from making comments.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Let's put this document on the overhead projector. It doesn't have to be admitted today, but I'd just like to ask for the witness's assistance by asking him whether he knows whether the 102nd Motorised Brigade was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, but I suppose you'll show it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That's north of Nedzarici, north of Dobrinja, and this is their document and shows the deployment of the 102nd Motorised Brigade. May I ask you to take a look at what it says above, the "Oslobodjenje" building. You mentioned that building as being one of the ones destroyed. Let me just tell everybody here that the "Oslobodjenje" building was the building belonging to the daily newspaper called "Oslobodjenje." Do you see that? There's a triangle there, number 3, and there's a semicircle there too. Have you found it? Right in the middle, it says "Nedzarici, Vojnicko Polje," and then there's an arrow, and then there's a sort of triangular flag for the battalion command.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Starting from Novi Grad -- we can start from Novi Grad. It will be simpler then to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see the building where it says "Oslobodjenje"?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see it, not for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that triangular flag with the number 3 on it, which was the headquarters of the 3rd Battalion, right in the middle of this picture? It says "3 mth"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, do you see that towards the bottom of that flag, it says "Oslobodjenje"?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now I can see it better on the map and not on what appears on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Witness, that this building, the "Oslobodjenje" building, had -- is where the Staff of the 3rd Battalion and the 102nd Motorised Brigade was, with a rocket-launcher there, because this arrow with the semicircle denotes that kind of weapon, a rocket-launcher?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have two comments to make here. On the one hand, and I already said so, this type of arms, such as rocket-launchers, were not kept in the same place. Secondly, I lived for six months and I was living just across the road from "Oslobodjenje," and I went there on several occasions. I never saw any Bosnian military. That is all I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you know that almost 80 per cent of the Bosnian soldiers were without uniforms, they were wearing civilian clothes? And that's according to their information. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, most of them liked to wear certain insignia, especially the chiefs. And, on the other hand, to come back to "Oslobodjenje," the shelling of "Oslobodjenje" happened at a very early stage of the conflict, so I don't know whether at that time there was already a staff of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And if I tell you that Nedzarici, and you know of Nedzarici - they're small buildings, just three floors - that they were shot at from the "Oslobodjenje" building, they were heavily fired at? Would you accept that? So from Vojnicko Polje, but particularly from the "Oslobodjenje" building, they came under very heavy fire?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible. We were close to the confrontation line. I know the place you're referring to, since I personally was kept for three hours in one of these small houses by one of your so-called people who were military who were responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that all these points, on the assumption that they've been correctly introduced onto this map, that they're all legitimate targets?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you call a legitimate target?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Legitimate military targets. Each of these points along the separation line, they're trenches, the positions of their staffs and headquarters, logistics, cannon positions, rocket positions. Are those all legitimate targets, as far as their adversaries are concerned?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you declare a target as being a military target, it can be subjected to a military action on the part of the person who's interested in such a target.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we lower the image to see "BRAG 102," the brigade artillery group of the 102nd Brigade with 18 artillery pieces, mortars and anti-aircraft, machine-guns, and Howitzers, so to the east where it says "Kovac." Brijesce Brdo, Brijesce Hill, do you see a strong concentration there? It's at an elevation of about 700 metres, dominating over the whole area with artillery pieces belonging to the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the moment, I don't see anything. So could you please be more precise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we proceed further, who drew this map, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a map. It's in the Latin script, a map belonging to the Muslim army, the 102nd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I question the provenance of the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that's why I'm asking. What you said is "a map belonging to the Muslim army." I don't follow, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a map showing the deployment of the 102nd Brigade of the Muslim army. And from all the documents, we know that that was what it was like, but this is their map, the one they use to follow their own activities. But in the documents, we shall see that all this is correct, and that that's where they're shooting from, and that that was the deployment of their forces. And it was common knowledge where the brigade was located, and the United Nations ought to know this because it was their job to know who was where.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So is it your position that you do not know who drew this map or marked this map?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Either the command or his deputy. But we received it, we obtained it -- well, it was seized in an action against the Muslims, the 102nd Brigade. We seized the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's proceed. What is your question? The witness was not able to identify the location you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, right up at the top, underneath the first three letters, "BOR," the "BOR" heading up at the top, you have a triangle with Howitzers, mortars. So underneath the title, "BOR," that's where you'll find the triangle, which is the artillery brigade group of the 102nd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that a legitimate target, in your opinion, then?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Chairman, I have two comments I would like to make.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then, on the other hand, I see that he is not quite consistent. On the one hand, he says that this is an authentic map, it is in Latin characters, so it can only come from the Bosnian Army, but for the three days I've been here, most of the documents and maps I've seen from the Serb Army -- Serbian Army were also in Latin characters, so I'm a bit at a loss.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But on the maps, themselves, the Serb commanders would write things on the maps in Cyrillic. Did you notice that? Right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. If you are concerned about the lines 10 to 15, that will be taken care of.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question, Witness. The commands of the adversary units, the command posts, are they legitimate targets? We can go through this very quickly if you give us yes-or-no answers.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command posts or the places where command posts are, that is, of course, a military target, but the Rules of War mean that normally we have to try and avoid collateral damage, as it is called.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the answer to the second question. The first question is about logistics bases. Are they legitimate targets?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A military logistic base is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So can I take them all together and say -- and ask whether the logistics centres, for example, the communications centres, all military installations, are they all legitimate military targets?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as it is military, it will be a military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about all the points along this separation line; are all those legitimate targets, all the trenches or parts of the trenches, et cetera? Are they all legitimate targets?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trenches are organisations for defence purposes. Obviously, they will be military targets.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we now have 1D1293 displayed, please. And it's a map. Just look at it briefly, and we've already displayed it. And we've just got a few more documents if I'm not given more time, but it's a great pity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you have 15 minutes to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D1293, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you believe that this is only a part of the legitimate targets, or, rather, military facilities in this part of the city? The 10th and 9th Mountain Brigades were not taken into account here, so do you know that in depth, behind the lines, right in the -- deep into the town, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that there were military installations all over the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton, line 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That map, as displayed, Your Honour, in my submission, is assuming facts not in evidence yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to tender this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm not quite -- speaking for myself, I'm not quite satisfied the witness has offered a foundation for this map, annotated map, to be admitted. What the witness said, it's possible there were military installations all over the city, and you'll have another opportunity to --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add something. I have even further doubts, since I see that there's no military installation noted along the front-line on the northern part of the city. So I think it might be a slightly biased presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I return this map to the Defence, the Prosecution is minded to take a look at it. Yes, please, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, I said, and this was confirmed by an international witness, that this is only a part of the installations, and one day we'll be offering up a complete map of all the military targets both along the front-line and in depth. So this is only some of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is yet again unnecessary comment on you, and you cannot complain about the shortage of time. You have 10 minutes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Witness, while we are still looking at this map, let me ask you this -- or, rather, the other map would be better. But do you agree that to the north of Sarajevo, we had the 2nd Corps of the BH Army, in the west the 3rd Zenica Corps, and to the south the 4th Mostar Corps of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I no longer remember which corps was at stake because I was not concerned about that. I was only interested in the elements of the 1st Corps, which was stationed inside the city of Sarajevo, itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, do you find it acceptable that at the beginning of the war, the separation line in town was 42 kilometres' long and that towards the end of the war the 1st Corps expanded to cover 64 kilometres? And that comes from their sources, that at the beginning there was 42 kilometres and at the end of the war 64 kilometres of line, front-line.

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not at Sarajevo at the end of the war, so I cannot know what happened at that point in time. But the 40-odd kilometres to which you refer which were there when I was present, that seems plausible. I think that was also the figure I remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we now have 1D479, but for that we'll have to go into private session. Is it the closed session, private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now we are in open session. Thank you. I take it you've concluded your cross-examination. We'll not admit this document, for the same reasons. Ms. Edgerton, before you begin your redirect examination, Judge Baird has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Witness, there is a matter on which I would like some clarification, but I think we should go into closed session for that, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Witness, I don't have too many things to ask you relating to the evidence you've previously given, but I'll begin. First of all, the day before yesterday you said, at page 4237, lines 15 to 17: "Vrbanja Bridge was the location where a French position of UNPROFOR was attacked by Serb troops that were wearing UN uniforms, and so this is what happened there." Do you recall saying this?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I was pointing to a time when I wasn't there, but I'm sure that another witness will be in a better position to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what period was that; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about 1995, what was preceded or what was simultaneous to our hostage-taking done by the Serbian Army against the UNPROFOR troops or staff.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On what, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness is speaking about things where he was not present, and I have no chance to test that. If another witness will testify to that, then there is no need to discuss it with this witness. I was not able to get an answer even about things where he was personally present, let alone things that he did not attend himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You can move on to another topic, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Witness, do you recall, from yesterday's proceedings, a discussion at pages 4255, lines 18 to 25, and onward to page 4260, about a Sarajevo Romanija Corps daily combat report, dated 31 May 1995, from which you were read a passage at page 4255, lines 22 to 24, by Dr. Karadzic? And I'll read you the passage. It said: "At 1015 hours, the enemy fired a 155-millimetre shell from Igman on the direction of Krivoglavci and Reljevo sectors." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I asked for the sectors to be showed on the map to me, and this did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Then could I ask, please, if we have P1052, which you viewed earlier in your testimony, brought up on the screen, please. I'd like to show you a map. We could have full-screen display. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall viewing this map, Witness, that appears on the screen, earlier in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I believe that it's on this map that I marked the artillery positions of the Serbian Army, the ones that I had witnessed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Perhaps now we can go from there to 65 ter 11789, which is a cut-out and enlargement from this very map. Pardon me, 11789G. Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you see an enlarged image on the map in front of you, Witness?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's on the western side of Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could I direct your attention to the upside-down Y shape in the road just to the left of where you see the name "Vogosca," do you see the place name Krivoglavci marked there?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if you go slightly further down the map, beside the blue letters "Bosna," just directly underneath the place Krivoglavci, do you see the place marked "Reljevo" marked to the left?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, do these markings on this map at the location most closest to Krivoglavci signify anything to you?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Markings? Oh, I see, right. As Mr. Karadzic showed it, these are on artillery location -- it's above Krivoglavci, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now, yesterday, without having seen this map, you were asked, at page 4257, lines 15 to 17: "If I tell you the fire from Mount Igman is directed exclusively at the north, towards Serb neighbourhoods of Sarajevo, does that sound plausible to you?" And you agreed: "Without a doubt." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KDZ-185 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I had no reference on the map. But now that you are showing me those markings, and if they correspond to what has been said yesterday by Mr. Karadzic, we can see that they were not directed at Serbian neighbourhoods, but they were perhaps Serbian artillery positions that were the targets.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. With those comments, I wonder if this cut-out from P1052 could be entered as an associated exhibit to P1052.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Cut-out and zoomed in?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It is, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it as a separate exhibit. I will consult the Court Deputy as to the practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit it separately.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1078, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I have just one more question. But as it was dealt with yesterday -- or the area that I wish to explore was dealt with yesterday in private session, could we move into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That concludes the re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Witness. That concludes your evidence. Thank you again for your coming to the Tribunal to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There are certain matters I was advised on your part to raise, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honour. It's about the status of a number of the associated exhibits to the statements which were admitted under seal, and I wonder if I can just go through the status of those exhibits by 65 ter number, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
