utterances.text: And it's -- what I wish to do is request that 65 ter 09578, which is an associated exhibit provisionally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The letter, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- entered as P1054, be under seal. And I'll just list the numbers, if I may. P1055, the same, P1059, P1060, P1061, P1062, P1065, and P1066.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We note your request. Since I have no P numbers with me at this moment, we'll come back to you if there's any problems. Also, I'll hear from the accused, if you have any problem with taking those things under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, if the motivation for putting them under seal was that they were under seal in the original case when they were admitted, then we would probably have no objection to that. But otherwise, absent any link between the testimony in open session and these particular documents, we don't see why they need to be under seal simply by the fact of their existence or link with the witness, if that link was never dealt with in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider the matter over the break. And there are two other administrative matters we can deal with at this moment. It's about Mr. Philipps, the associated documents. The 29th of June, the Prosecution requested leave to reply to the accused's response regarding the documents submitted through Mr. Philipps. Because the Chamber believes that a reply will assist the Chamber in deciding the motion and is satisfied that it would be in the interest of justice, so we hereby grant leave for the Prosecution to do so. And, finally, the 28th of June, Mr. Karadzic requested the assistance of a Defence expert, Mr. Subotic, in the courtroom during the testimony of Mr. Suljevic. The Prosecution did not oppose this request. In light of the anticipated technical nature of Mr. Suljevic's testimony, we will permit the presence of Dr. Subotic in the courtroom during that testimony. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I missed one administrative matter. I'm reminded of it, Your Honour. The day before yesterday, at pages 4204 to 4205, we used 65 ter 13637 with the witness, and it's a blow-up and translation of part of P1021, and I've been recommended to ask that that be attached to 13637 -- sorry, that it be attached to 1021 as a translation of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Excuse me, Mr. President. We have one small administrative matter also. We are finally able to report that one of the MFI documents, MFI D195, has been translated. The translation has been attached and up-loaded into e-court, and we would ask that that now be admitted as a full exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll consider the matter and then issue a ruling in due course. Thank you. We'll have a break for 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Mandic. Welcome to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I greet you, Your Honours, and greet the Prosecutor and Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I was advised that you have something to address the Chamber before you begin your testimony, Mr. Mandic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your permission, I would like to address the Court with a few words. I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to allow me to be a witness of the Court and not of the Prosecution, and that is what I explained and requested in a letter. I think that you can issue subpoenas for those who do not wish to testify, which is not my case. I do wish to testify before this honourable and august Chamber to tell you everything I knew -- I know, because of the truth and justice. But I don't wish to say these things as a Prosecution witness, who imposed this status on me, regardless of my will. And they threatened me, the associates of Mr. Tieger. They told me that if I didn't come in to testify, I would be incarcerated. Now, why do I not want to be a Prosecution witness? Because in 2003 I was suspected of aiding and abetting and hiding Dr. Karadzic. I spent five months because of that in a solitary confinement cell in Belgrade, and none of my family members could visit me. And The Hague investigators came to see me. The Prosecutor's investigator, that is, were allowed to come and see me. They asked me about the whereabouts of Mr. Karadzic, his health, and everything else that they were interested in knowing about him. Now, on several occasions, I was told that if I failed to co-operate and failed to tell them where Dr. Karadzic was, that I would be an accused before this Court and that I would be accused and found guilty by a Serbian Court. However, five months later, I was released without any criminal proceedings being taken against me. And until the present day, the state of Serbia has not apologised to me for keeping me in prison. After that, I was kidnapped, as a citizen of Montenegro, and transferred in the space of two hours to a prison in Sarajevo, without any extradition proceedings or anything else. And in the prison there and in the Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the evening hours I was taken out and was interrogated by the operatives and investigators of The Hague Tribunal, or, rather, the OTP, or the security services who were down there in Sarajevo, and mostly they asked me, once again, about Dr. Karadzic, his whereabouts, his movements, his state of health, and so on and so forth. Of course, I wasn't able to assist the OTP by telling them anything, because from 1996 I have had nothing to do with Dr. Karadzic. I wasn't in contact with him at all. I tried to present my arguments and to explain this to them, but they just didn't want to listen. And then these operatives, the investigators, told me that I would be taken to court in Bosnia-Herzegovina and that the prosecutor of the BH Court would raise an indictment against me, and that I would be sentenced to a prison term of eight years. When I said that they had no grounds for filing a lawsuit against me, they said that they would find grounds and that that wasn't important. So everything that -- during that evening, when they interviewed me, everything those operatives told me would happen did happen. I was prosecuted because of the commercial bank in Srpsko Sarajevo, which is owned by me, that I provided credits and loans to firms and companies which assisted Dr. Karadzic. And I was found guilty and given a prison term of eight years. I served five years. And I was accused of aiding one of the suspects of The Hague Tribunal, the accused, actually, Radovan Karadzic. And after I was acquitted after 2003, I was placed on a blacklist and prohibited from entering into the European Union countries and the United States because I was suspected of assisting Dr. Karadzic and financing him and hiding him. Although that decision was taken in 2007, I am still on that list, on that blacklist, and at all the airports of the European Union, the Montenegrin-Serbian border, Croatian border, and so on, I am always taken into custody by the police, I am interrogated by them, and then I'm sent back. If I'm going to Bosnia -- from Bosnia, I'm sent back to Bosnia, and so on. And that was the situation quite recently when I testified in the Stanisic trial. I spent one and a half hours in Vienna, in the Office for Immigrants, or whatever it's called, and I was interrogated there. Yesterday, they kept me back at the airport for one hour, at the Amsterdam Airport, although there was a subpoena from this honourable Tribunal and a safe passage permit. The driver waited for me, he explained the situation, but that's what happened. So I considered -- well, let alone the fact that my two sons were held in custody. And John Ruttel, one of the investigators, said to my son that he would be released if I were to come to Sarajevo, so that's what happened to me. Of course, when I served tow-thirds of my sentence in prison and left prison, it was established that I was found guilty of a crime that didn't exist and that it was all bureaucracy and false testimony on the part of false witnesses. And as an American citizen who had immunity, this person went to Texas, to Dallas, Texas, and she even took some money from my bank. I was helpless, faced with a situation of that kind. And Dr. Karadzic has been in a Scheveningen prison for two or three years. I had no contact with him whatsoever, but I remain somebody who was prosecuted and found guilty and held in prison for seven or eight years, and my family suffered. And now, as such, I am supposed to come here and be here as a Prosecution witness, whereas the Prosecution thought that I was harbouring him and assisting him. I think that that is not commensurate with man's dignity, and I would like to request that the Trial Chamber allow me to be a Court witness. But I will accept your ruling and decision. And I say this -- I set this out in my letter, because I really do not wish to be a Prosecution witness. However, if you order that to be the case, then I will comply. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you raised several issues, but I will address only those which relate to the Tribunal's business; i.e., your testimony. Anybody, any citizen in the world, is obliged to give evidence once subpoenaed. So as a matter of law, you are obligated to give evidence as subpoenaed. But it is a separate matter for the Chamber to allow you to give evidence as a Chamber witness, as a witness of the Court, as you put it. Having said that, I'd like to hear from the parties, what position they take in relation to allow the witness to give evidence as a Chamber witness. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Well, I believe, in this instance, we're talking about a distinction without a difference. I think the witness has made it abundantly clear that he's not here as a, quote/unquote, "Prosecution witness," whatever he believes that to mean. He's here to give evidence. He happens to be called -- or he happens to have been called during this phase of the case, but he made it clear he wishes not to be identified with the Prosecution, he wishes to give evidence to the Court. That's been made clear; one way or another, he would be here. So whatever designation we choose to give Mr. Mandic in this instance, his position would not change. It would be clear to everyone. And I think the procedural approach would remain the same. I think we are -- everyone would expect the questioning to be elicited first from the Prosecution and then from the Defence. So it appears to me that the point that Mr. Mandic wished to make has been made, and I'm not sure what further measures would be necessary in this instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic or Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we had a similar -- actually, an identical request from Lord Owen in the pre-trial stage of this case, and he requested to be called as a Chamber witness. And the ruling was that he could be called as a Prosecution witness simply because the Prosecution goes first. In that instance, we said we would have called Lord Owen if the Prosecution didn't. In this instance, definitely we would have called Mr. Mandic if the Prosecution didn't, so it's only because the Prosecution goes first that he's here as a Prosecution witness. And I think with that understanding, we all just expect him to tell the truth, no matter what the designation, and hope that he'll do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, you should be aware of the consequence -- the legal consequence if he's allowed to testify as a Chamber witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: As far as I understand the legal consequence, in terms of the procedure, would be that essentially the Chamber would either ask him to give his evidence in response to Chamber questions or in response to his own statement, and then the parties would be examining him after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And entitled to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct. And we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: May be allowed to put leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I understand the Prosecutor could possibly put leading questions to him at that point. But that's up to the Chamber, how you like to control your proceedings. As far as we're concerned, he's here because the Prosecution goes first, and so we think that that procedure is satisfactory to us. But if you prefer to have him testify in another procedure, we don't mind that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, since there seems to be some consideration given to that, I would simply note the Court does have available Mr. Mandic's previous testimony, and is aware of his appearance in Stanisic/Zupljanin as well, so that probably gives the Court a little more information about how it might wish to proceed and what procedural steps it could implement if it chose to adopt one of the options.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, we have heard your request, that you be considered to be a witness of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a request, just a request, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. You request that you be considered to be a witness of the Court, rather than of the Prosecution, and in this regard I would like to note the following: In the system which operates at this Tribunal, witnesses are called by the Prosecution and the Defence to give evidence. The evidence that is given by such witnesses is, however, evidence provided to the Chamber and for consideration and analysis by the Chamber in reaching its conclusions concerning the charges against the accused. In this respect, evidence is evidence, and it is of no consequence which party brought the particular witness to give it. However, as a matter of procedure, it is the party who calls a witness who normally first asks questions in what we call examination-in-chief. Then the opposing party cross-examines the witness. The Chamber can choose at any point to put its own questions to the witness, but in general the questioning is performed by the Prosecution and the Defence. Under our Rules, a Chamber may also order the parties to produce evidence and may, itself, call witnesses to give testimony. We are happy to hear that you are prepared to -- well, in your situation, at the request of the Prosecution, the Chamber issued a subpoena directing you to appear today to begin your testimony, and we are grateful to hear that you are prepared to do so. However, noting your concern not to be considered as a witness for the Prosecution, and the comments that I have just made, we are prepared to consider you as a witness of the Court. However, in the interests of the best presentation of your evidence, you will be questioned first by the Prosecution and then by the accused, Mr. Karadzic, and I would ask you, that you answer all of those questions to the best of your ability. The Chamber may also intervene from time to time to ask questions of you. But that said, I would like you first to take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shall I stand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please have a seat. One further administrative matter, Mr. Tieger. This witness was supposed to give his evidence partially pursuant to Rule 92 ter. Are you happy to go live with this witness or do you like me to check with the witness he would stick by his previous testimony in Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, we intend to present his evidence, in part, through 92 ter. And I would note, as the Court will hear momentarily, that that is precisely what happened just about a month ago in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case. So I think that would be an appropriate way to proceed, the most efficient way, and then we can -- there will be a great deal of live evidence in addition, but I think that certainly the manner we intended to proceed, it was a manner in which the case proceeded earlier, and I think it's a most efficient manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, sometime in 2004, during November and December, you gave testimony -- you testified in the case Prosecutor versus Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity to go through the transcript of your evidence in that case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did that before I testified in the Stanisic and Zupljanin trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you confirm with me that that transcript accurately reflects your statement, and if asked again, you would say the same answers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I do confirm that. I confirm everything that I said in the Momcilo Krajisnik trial, with the changes that I made, and told Prosecutor Korner and was introduced in those proceedings during the Stanisic/Zupljanin trial, those amendments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Has this Chamber been provided with those corrections, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to adduce those orally. I can do so now, if the Court would wish, or I can direct the Court to the appropriate transcript pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So with the consent of the Defence, I will leave it to you to go through the corrections later on when you examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd be happy to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I never did this practice. Do I need to ask further questions? I think we did all the requirements of Rule 92 ter. And then on that basis, we'll admit his transcript as a Chamber exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 22487 will be Exhibit C2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger or Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Mandic. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Perhaps it's best to begin by focusing on the corrections you made in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case to your testimony in the Krajisnik case. And I believe there were three of them. The first, which appears at page 9401 of the Stanisic/Zupljanin transcript, was in connection with a document you reviewed concerning the number of Muslim civilians who passed through the facility at Kula, and the testimony was that the documents -- the questioning in the Krajisnik case was at page 8742. The testimony was: "According to rough estimates, about 10.000 Muslim civilians of all ages passed through this facility during the war, spending between several days and a few months in this facility." That's what the document said. Your answer was: "It was two years after I left for Belgrade, and it was the president of the Central Commission for Exchanges of POWs, Ljubisa Vladusic." And then you essentially indicated that you didn't challenge the document. And then you wanted to make a correction to the civilians who were referenced in that document, the 10.000 Muslim civilians of all ages who passed through the facility. So if you want to make that correction now, I invite you to do so.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, this is correct. During the testimony in the Krajisnik trial, I was shown a letter from Mr. Bulajic, who was president of the Central Commission for the Exchange of Prisoners, and Mr. Vladusic, Ljubisa Vladusic, who was the head of the Office for Refugees or Committee for Refugees, or whatever it was called. Now, in that letter they stated - and it was sent to the government - that during the war, through the buildings, or, rather, the premises of the Butmir Correction Centre in Eastern Sarajevo, that about 10.000 non-Serbs passed through. That is to say, that referred to prisoners of war and civilians and people who were taken away from the areas engulfed by war, and all those who spent from two to three days to several months there. And I said, during that testimony and during the testimony during the Stanisic/Zupljanin trial, that there was no reason for me not to believe those figures and that there was a great deal of fluctuation in that particular location because it was at the separation line between the area held by the Muslim forces and Serb forces, and where the prisoners were exchanged, whether POWs or civilians who were in various areas of Republika Srpska and the federation, brought to that place and exchanged. And it was according to the all-for-all principle, and it was near Sarajevo Airport. That's why I said that I had no doubt -- no reason to doubt it, especially since after 1992 I didn't have any insight into the fluctuation and migration of these people who, during 1991 and 1992, took shelter in Dobrinja from the war, when there were conflicts between the Serb and Muslim forces. So in my view, those two statements are identical, the statement made in the Krajisnik trial and in the Stanisic/Zupljanin trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The second -- the second correction, Mr. Mandic, can be found at page 9405 of the Stanisic/Zupljanin testimony, and I believe you were correcting a portion of the Krajisnik transcript at pages 8945 through 46, and you wanted to focus on the length of time that the MUP could keep people in detention. And the question at page 9405 from Ms. Korner was: "But, anyhow, you're saying, are you, that at no stage did the length of time which the MUP could keep people -- could keep people in detention for change [Realtime transcript read in error "exchange"] to longer than three days?" And your answer was: "Correct." So is it accurate that there was a discussion in the Krajisnik case which indicated that the -- the possibility of a provision according to which detention could last up to 31 days, and you corrected that by saying that at no stage did the length of time which the MUP could keep people for change to longer than three days?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: It's not correct, Mr. Tieger. We weren't talking about people who were supposed to be exchanged. It was the pre-trial proceedings for those who were suspected of having committed certain crimes, and their detention according to the Law on Criminal Procedure, which was up to three days, that is to say, 70 hours. So we weren't talking about people who were up for exchange, but suspects in regular procedures for individual crimes. And that law was enforced in the former Yugoslavia, taken over by Republika Srpska and Bosnia-Herzegovina, because it was -- there was just one criminal code.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't believe I mentioned the word "exchange," but rather "detention." But in any event, Mr. Mandic, have you now accurately provided the information you wanted to about that issue?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Tieger. The interpretation I heard was "people kept for the exchange." That's why I reacted. It was probably down to the interpretation. But what you just stated is correct. Yes, people who could have been detained by the police in the pre-trial phase, according to the law governing criminal procedures, they could be detained for up to 72 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 76, line 18. Page 76, line 18, contains the word "exchange," so it wasn't the interpretation. That's what was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger said "detention for exchange."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in any event --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It can be checked against the recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine. As long as the correction is clear, I'm more than satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Mandic, the last correction I believe you made, but I leave it to you to tell us if it's otherwise, is in relation to testimony you gave which was at pages 8677 and 9314 through 15 about who instructed you to send the 31 March 1992 dispatch regarding the split of the MUP, that is, the split of the police. And you explained in your testimony, at pages 9405 through 9406 in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case: "I wrote the dispatch. It was logical for the minister of the interior to instruct me to do this, but he did not. I was in charge of the Serbs in the MUP at the time and did not write this dispatch on anyone's behalf. I received information from Velibor Ostojic that the law had been passed in accordance with the Cutileiro Plan, and I wrote this on my own initiative in accordance with my own conscience and professionalism and in co-operation with the professionals in my cabinet." Now, Mr. Mandic, there was further discussion about that during the course of the Stanisic/Zupljanin case, including at what point you came to that decision about -- that it was a mistake, whether it was before or after talking to the Defence, where Mico Stanisic was at the time the dispatch was written, and so on. So I leave it up to you to tell the Court whether or not any further correction is required. But that seemed to be the point at which you made the correction in the Stanisic/Zupljanin case, so I'd ask you to let the Court know if that is the correction you wish to make and if there's any further elaboration necessary.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I will, for the benefit of the Court, explain this in a few words. As far as the writing of the dispatch is concerned, nobody gave me instructions, as the assistant minister for the interior. On 23rd March, the "Official Gazette" published the Law on Internal Affairs. Eight days later, it came into effect. I was informed of that by Velibor Ostojic, the minister of information. And then I wrote that dispatch, which is in keeping with that law and in keeping with the Constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Mr. Stanisic had, therefore, nothing to do with it. And at that time, having forgotten all these details, which didn't mean much to me, I remembered that I contacted directly with the minister of the interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, that's not the case. Mr. Stanisic had nothing to do with it. The rest is as I testified in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Mandic, is it accurate, then, that those are the corrections and the only corrections you wish to make to your testimony in the Krajisnik case?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, Mr. Mandic, perhaps we can begin, although --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, given that the whole bunch of his testimony was introduced in the form of written form, in writing, unless the Defence is opposed, for the benefit of the public the Chamber is minded to ask you to read out the summary of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Mandic was the assistant minister of interior for Bosnia and Herzegovina from 1991 until April 1992. After the outbreak of the conflict, Mr. Mandic was, for a short period, the deputy minister -- or served as a deputy to Mr. Mico Stanisic for the Serbian Ministry of the Interior, before becoming the minister of justice for Republika Srpska on 19 May 1992. From December --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. 12th May, at the Assembly meeting in Banja Luka, I was appointed on the 12th of May, not the 19th of May. That's certain. It must be a typo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: From December 1992 to 1994, Mr. Mandic served as the director of the Bureau of Republika Srpska in Belgrade. Mr. Mandic was the SDS nominee or selection for assistant minister of interior in the pre-war period, selected by Radovan Karadzic and Rajko Dukic, who was the president of the Executive Board of the SDS and the head of the Personnel Comission. Part of Mr. Mandic's responsibilities was to ensure that SDS selections for positions in the MUP were realised, and he frequently spoke about this with the accused and other SDS leaders.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Mr. Tieger. It was not about selections; it was about implementing the agreement between the winning parties, and that agreement was on how, according to national representation, senior posts would be distributed. It was first Zepinic who was in charge of that, and then I took over. At the beginning, Zepinic was the main personnel man on the Serbian side in the MUP, and then I took over that role. It was about appointing the candidates put forward by the winning national parties to various executive posts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On February 11th, 1992, leading Serb members of the MUP were informed by Mico Stanisic about a decision of the Council of Ministers concerning, quote, "the establishment of Serb MUPs in municipalities where there was a majority Serb population." And following this, Mr. Mandic informed Serb regional leaders in the MUP to move ahead with preparing a Serb MUP. Part of the preparation --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not correct, Mr. Tieger. I did not present it that way. On the 11th of February, there was a meeting of Serbian personnel in the joint MUP, where a dissatisfaction was expressed with the work of the joint MUP, and conclusions were adopted which are part of the documentation; maybe not in this case, but in the Stanisic and Zupljanin case and the Krajisnik case. And that meeting was not convened by Mico Stanisic, but by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't believe --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can go back to that document, and you can put questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We will return to that document, Mr. Mandic. Part of the preparation included arming Serb police and Serb police stations. On 31 March 1992, Mr. Mandic sent a dispatch to all Serbian police officers, instructing them, in accordance with decisions of the Serb Assembly and the Council of Ministers, to split the MUP, the joint MUP, along ethnic lines. The National Security Council or NSC was established in April 1992, composed of Bosnian Serb leaders and presided over by the accused. On the 24th of April, 1992, the NSC decided that the Ministry of Justice would assume responsibilities for the exchange of prisoners after the organs of the Ministry of Interior had completed its work. This decision resulted in the establishment on 8 May 1992 of a commission for exchange of prisoners of war and detained persons. Mr. Mandic confirmed that non-Serb civilians, in addition to alleged combatants, were detained and exchanged into non-Serb areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Tieger. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I get the interpretation correctly, "prisoners of war." However, in the transcript, I read just "prisoners." And we put it earlier that when we say in our language "prisoner," it implies prisoners of war. Nobody exchanged convicts. We exchanged prisoners of war. But this has to be clear, and ask the interpreters, if you will, whether it's true that "the prisoner" means not a convict, but somebody who was detained in combat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. At line 15, I see "prisoners of war," but let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Collection centres or camps were established in Republika Srpska. Mr. Mandic testified that a number of these collection centres detained women, children, and persons who did not take part in the war. This was, in part, a result of ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANDIC SAID
utterances.text: "The army set up collection centres, as did the police, and the police -- and the people from war-torn areas were brought there, and they were either exchanged or ethnic cleansing was conducted where there were no war operations." When shown a Ministry of Interior report of July 1992 with references to liberation of territories and mopping up, he said: "As far as I knew, these were combat operations carried on by the army, police, and these crisis staffs." And that: "I suppose these were combat operations and ethnic cleansing of non-Serb population in some areas." Referring to a series of intercepts and orders, Mr. Mandic confirmed that prisoners being detained by Bosnian Serb authorities were used for forced labour and that some Muslim prisoners were killed while performing this work. Mr. Mandic authenticated the intercept of a conversation he had with Branko Kvesic on 10 July, 1992, where Mr. Mandic said there is no sense in waging war now because: "... counties and national communities have already taken everything that was supposed to be taken." Mr. Mandic testified that by this statement, he was conveying the position of the state leadership of Republika Srpska; namely, the president, Dr. Karadzic. With respect to Sarajevo, Mr. Mandic stated that the ethnic division of Sarajevo was one of the political objectives of the Serbian leadership. Mr. Mandic confirmed that when asked in a telephone conversation in April whether Sarajevo would be divided, he replied that the Sarajevo problem would be solved by war and then sit down to talk, and that reflected the attitude of the Bosnian Serb political leadership at the time. He also stated that the way in which the Sarajevo problem was to be solved by war was explained when he said: "We're waiting for them to come from Lisbon. The alternative is an old one. We defeat Sarajevo and we expel them all the way to Visoko." Mr. Mandic said that Mr. Karadzic was aware of activities on the ground, stating that: "Police and military structures informed him about what was going on in the territory." When asked whether the government made known to the Presidency its concerns about irregularities and inhumane treatment in detention facilities and camps, Mr. Mandic said: "Yes, that was communicated on a daily basis." Mr. Mandic testified that a 17 July 1992 Ministry of Interior document sent to the accused and to the prime minister reported that: "The army, crisis staffs, and war presidencies have requested that the army round up or capture as many Muslim civilians as possible." He also confirmed that the information contained in that document, including the fact that conditions in camps were poor and some persons were not observing international norms, reflected the kind of information available at the time. Mr. Mandic said that the government established a commission to visit: "... facilities, prisons, collection centres, and other facilities where POWs were sheltered or people who had undergone ethnic cleansing and who were held by the army and the police." Mr. Mandic testified that in Republika Srpska: "The absolute number one was Dr. Radovan Karadzic, without a contest." The second-most powerful person was Momcilo Krajisnik. Nobody could enter government without the permission of Karadzic and Krajisnik, and for government positions they selected only people they could trust. Radovan Karadzic, as president of the republic, was the supreme military commander. And, Your Honour, with the Court's permission, I'll proceed with the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, perhaps it's only fair to begin by providing the Court with a bit more detail about your background, although I know it's contained in the transcript. But it's useful and it shouldn't take long. You attended the Police Academy in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then you worked for the SUP in Sarajevo; that is, the local police?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: In the city police force of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then you attended university, where you read law; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I worked and studied at the same time --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: -- and graduated from the Faculty of Law within three and a half years.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After graduation, it's correct that you became a judge of the Basic Court?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I passed the Bar exam, and then after the Olympic Games in Sarajevo I became a judge of the Regular Court in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you served as a judge until 1991, when you became an assistant minister of the Bosnian MUP or Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Early in 1991, at the proposal of Vitomir Zepinic, I went to the head office of the Serbian Democratic Party, where he nominated me or proposed me to Rajko Dukic, then head of the Executive Board and main personnel man, and it was said that the SDS would nominate me for head of serve for crime prevention. And that was the first time I saw Mr. Karadzic ever, my first contact with him. And then he said - I remember this well - we need good, honourable policemen of Serbian ethnicity who will take into their hands law enforcement, protect the lives and property of citizens. And in all other matters concerning my appointment, I communicated with Vitomir Zepinic and Rajko Dukic. And Zepinic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't get whether Rajko Dukic or Zepinic was then already appointed assistant minister for police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay, I think we can move on with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In April of 1992, Mr. Mandic, you began to serve in the Bosnian Serb MUP, after the split of the police, and you served effectively as deputy to Mico Stanisic, as the deputy minister of the interior, is that correct, for a brief time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: It was the Government of the socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, headed by Jure Pelivan, relieved me of my duties as assistant minister on 5 April 1992. In that period between the 10th and the 25th April, I was at Vrace and I worked on the duties of assistant head of the Serbian police. And although I was without any job at the time, Mico Stanisic gave me certain duties at Vrace. And waiting for a letter of appointment, I was informed, and you mentioned it a moment ago, Mr. Tieger, at the session of the Council for National Security, or whatever that body was called, I was invited to come to Pale on the 24th of April, where I was told that the first minister of justice, the first Serbian minister of justice, Ranko Nikolic, did not appear at work, and that I would take his job. And that was on the 16th of May in Banja Luka, when I was appointed in his stead as the first Serbian minister of justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to avoid the risk of any confusion, Mr. Mandic: There is a suggestion in your answer, and I want to clarify that, that you were -- that you only went to work for the Republika Srpska MUP because you were relieved of your responsibilities as assistant minister for the joint MUP.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: No, not only that. I went of my own goodwill to Vrace, but I had been relieved of my duties in the joint MUP, because the agreement had been that appending the solution of status problems of all the employees, those employees, especially executive employees, should remain in their posts. On the 7th of April, I came to work in the joint MUP, when I was given an official document relieving me of my duties, and then I reported to Mico Stanisic. But the agreement had been that all the senior people in the joint MUP should stay in their posts until the whole situation in the republic and in the Ministry of Police is resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic, you served as the minister of justice until November of 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: 23rd November 1992, until the session of the Assembly in Zvornik. I believe that was the 23rd of November, when Mr. Branko Zeric [phoen] resigned as prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And from there, you went on to be the director of the Bureau of the Republika Srpska in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I was head of the bureau, not director. But never mind. It was a bureau of the Government of Republika Srpska, and then it grew into a bureau of Republika Srpska. It covered all forms of assistance to the people and the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, people who came to Belgrade; the wounded, veterans, disabled people who fled the war zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just to round it out finally, and I think you indicated that to the Court earlier, you were appointed as and served as the director of the Privredna Banka?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: In November 1995, I was appointed director of Privredna Banka in Serbian Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And who appointed you to that position?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: The board of directors of the bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I believe in your testimony in Krajisnik, you attributed your appointment to Mr. Krajisnik. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: No. He suggested that I should accept that position. According to the Law on Banks, however, it was the board of directors that took that decision. But since I was left without my job in the bureau, because I believe Mr. Karadzic relieved me of that, Karadzic -- sorry, Krajisnik suggested that I take this post, and I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'm going to mention one last thing, Mr. Mandic, because it's been mentioned in every -- in both the Stanisic/Zupljanin case and in the Krajisnik case. You were also known for your sporting activities in Sarajevo and in Bosnia, correct, and that was as a judo expert?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a sportsman, judo. I have a lot of medals on the Yugoslav level and the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I continued with that until the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just a couple of minutes, Mr. Mandic, so I want to just begin with one topic, and that's relatively, chronologically, at the time of your work with the joint MUP and your position as assistant minister in the joint MUP. First of all, it's correct, isn't it, that the composition -- the ethnic composition of the joint MUP at that time was approximately 75 per cent Serb; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: I don't believe there was 70 per cent Serbs in the police, but it was disproportionate to the national composition of Bosnia. I believe there were around 2.000 Serbs on the police force, and that was higher than the representation of Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, at page 8650 in the course of the Krajisnik case, you said: "Up until the beginning of the war, in the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were about 11.000 members of the MUP"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And: "From among them -- or among them, there were 75 per cent Serbs"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: It must be a mistake. That's not so, Mr. Tieger. There were 2.000 Serb policemen more than their percentage in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's what we established in 1991. And I believe I explained that in the 1960s and the 1970s, it was mostly Serbs who joined the army and the police. It was a difficult job, a hard job, and the other two ethnic communities did not favour it, so Serb young men were the majority candidates for military and police academies, for purely social reasons, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll check the numbers on that over the evening. But it is correct, then, as you stated in Krajisnik, that in Bosnia and Herzegovina it was mainly Serbs who were in the army and police, which did not correspond to the ethnic pattern of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: That means, as we put it, the Serbs happily joined the police in those years, the 1970s, because they lived in backward areas, mainly raised cattle. They lived in poverty, and this was a job that helped them provide for their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I did find the reference I was looking for, if I could have one minute more, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that was at page 9338 of Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: During the cross-examination, you said: "I have to remind you, at the beginning, when the national parties only came into power, there were 10.000 employees in the Ministry of the Interior. I'm speaking only about the uniformed staff. Over 7.000 of them were Serbs, a little over 2.000 were Muslims, and very few were Croats."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MANDIC
utterances.text: If I said that, I was wrong. I'm sure that there were 2.000 Serbs relative -- 2.000 more Serbs than parity level, in terms of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know if I actually said that. But if I did, it's wrong. What is correct is what I said now. And, finally, it's possible to find, on the whole police force, how many men there were in total and how many were Serbs, Muslims, and Croats. There must be records.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour and Mr. Mandic, it's now time to adjourn. It's 7.00. And unless the Court has some further matter, I'll resume the questioning tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for today. Mr. Mandic, probably you must have been informed by other Chambers, but during the course of your testimony you are not supposed to discuss your evidence with anybody else. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll resume tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 1st day of July, 2010, at 9.00 a.m.
